[THOUGHT]  
The clinical picture remains highly consistent with **interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS)**. Key supportive features include:  
- Chronic (>5 months), progressive bladder/pelvic discomfort *between* voids, *relieved by urination*

The pending **cystoscopy with hydrodistension** is a pivotal diagnostic step. In IC/BPS, hydrodistension may reveal:  
• **Glomerulations** (petechial hemorrhages) — present in >90% of non-ulcerative IC/BPS cases *after* distension  
• **Hunner’s lesions** (triangular, erythematous, fibrotic mucosal patches) — pathognomonic for ulcerative IC/BPS (~5–10% of cases)

✓ Rule out malignancy, radiation cystitis, or other structural pathology  
✓ Identify Hunner’s lesions (which guide therapy — e.g., fulguration)  
✓ Support diagnosis when findings are classic (e.g., glomerulations post-hydrodistension)

• Document glomerulations (supportive, though nonspecific and dependent on technique/pressure)

3. **Rule out comorbidities**: Consider gynecologic evaluation for endometriosis (given dyspareunia and chronic pelvic pain) and gastroenterologic assessment if bowel symptoms emerge.  

No evidence to support acute infection, obstructive uropathy, neurogenic bladder, or malignancy at this time.

[THOUGHT]  
This updated summary reinforces and deepens the prior diagnostic impression. The symptom duration is now specified as >6 months (not just >6 weeks), indicating chronicity consistent with IC/BPS rather than transient or reactive cystitis. The progressive course further supports a neurogenic-sensory–myofascial disorder rather than an acute or self-limited process.
